title: Collections Review: Data Engineer
story: The final project for the collections unit: you're a data engineer at a startup. You have user events streaming in, product data to look up, and unique visitors to track. You need Vec for ordered data, Map for lookups, and Set for uniqueness — all working together. This is your data engineering interview question.
why: Real systems use multiple collection types simultaneously — Vec for event streams, Map for user profiles, Set for unique IDs — and orchestrating them together is the essence of backend engineering.
analogy: An analytics system is like a restaurant: the order tickets (Vec) come in sequence, the menu (Map) lets you look up dish names by ID, and the reservation list (Set) tracks unique guests — no duplicates. The host, chef, and server each use a different tool for their specific job.
try_it: Add a `filter_events_by_user` that returns all events for a specific user ID. Add `user_activity_report` that prints each user's name and how many events they triggered. Then add an `export_csv` function that produces a simple comma-separated string of all events. Bonus: add a `most_active_user` function using a frequency counter pattern.
tips: Choose Vec for ordered, sequential data (event logs, timelines, queues)
Choose Map for key-value associations (user profiles, configurations, caches)
Choose Set for uniqueness guarantees (visitor IDs, tags, permissions — anything where 'is it here?' matters)
common_mistakes: Using one collection type for everything — Vec for lookups (slow), Map for ordering (impossible without extra data)
Storing the same data in multiple collections without sync — if you remove from Vec, also remove from Map
Choosing a collection before analyzing access patterns — always ask: 'will I look up by key? need order? need uniqueness?'
